title: Counting words: normalized frequency, Zipf's law and keyness
summary: Turn raw counts into per-million frequencies and explain why tiny corpora mislead; say why a count needs a concordance before it means anything; describe Zipf's law; define keyness, compute a log-likelihood keyness score by hand, and read a keyword list the way Farr & Murphy (2009) do.
sourceNote: Week 5 Thursday slides (keyness), Week 6 overview (corpus statistics), Farr & Murphy 2009 'Religious references in contemporary Irish English' (the Monday reading), Benor & Levy 2006 (Wednesday reading). Dr. Kraus's Week 6 slides were not posted yet when this was written; recheck against them.

blocks.md: **The question** People say Irish English speakers use words like *God* and *Jesus* a lot, and mostly not about religion. Is that true, or just a stereotype? You can't answer that by asking people (they'll tell you what they *think* they say). You answer it by **counting** what they actually say, in a corpus, and comparing it with other speakers. That is exactly what Farr & Murphy (2009), your Monday reading, did.
blocks.label: why

blocks.md: **Why it matters outside class** Every 'word of the year', every dictionary's 'this word is informal' label, every spam filter and every authorship case (the Rowling example from Week 2) rests on the same move: count a word here, count it there, and ask whether the difference is real or just noise. This chapter is the toolkit for that.

sections.heading: Raw counts lie: normalize to per million

blocks.body: How many times a word occurs in a corpus. *God* occurs 785 times in the Limerick Corpus of Irish English (LCIE).
The count scaled to a common corpus size, usually **per million words**: `count ÷ corpus size × 1,000,000`. It lets you compare corpora of different sizes.

blocks.title: Why you must normalize
blocks.body:
Corpus A: 2,000,000 words, 'hell' occurs 200 times
Corpus B:   500,000 words, 'hell' occurs  80 times

Raw: A looks bigger (200 vs 80).
Per million:
  A = 200 ÷ 2,000,000 × 1,000,000 = 100 pm
  B =  80 ÷   500,000 × 1,000,000 = 160 pm

B actually uses 'hell' MORE often. Raw counts reward big corpora.

blocks.md: Farr & Murphy say it directly: their corpora 'vary in size from half a million words to two million words, and so results are normalized to words per million'. Every table in the paper is per million from then on.

blocks.body: Per million can make **tiny** corpora look impressive. Farr & Murphy's age groups are 15,000 words each. A score of **266 per million** there is 266 ÷ 1,000,000 × 15,000 = **4 actual occurrences**. One chatty speaker could produce all four. Always ask: how many raw hits is this?

blocks.prompt: A word occurs 12 times in a 60,000-word corpus. What is its frequency per million?

blocks.body: Every occurrence of a search word printed with its left and right context, one per line (*Key Word In Context*). It is how you read what the word is actually doing in each hit.

blocks.md: The count of *God* doesn't tell you whether someone is praying or saying *oh my God* about a football match. Farr & Murphy read the concordance lines and split each count into **religious** and **non-religious** use. In LCIE, only **146 of 1,528** religious references are used religiously: about 1 in 10.

blocks.title: Same words, opposite patterns (Farr & Murphy Tables 1 and 3)

blocks.md: The written/spoken flip is the finding: in writing these words are mostly religious, in speech mostly not. No frequency list could show that; the concordance did.

blocks.body: A sequence of words that recurs: *oh my God* (243 times in LCIE), *swear to God* (33), *thank God* (34). Looking left and right of a search word in the concordance is how you find them.

blocks.prompt: Why couldn't Farr & Murphy split the 3,500 hits in Table 2 into religious and non-religious uses?
blocks.answer: They say it was too much work and too often ambiguous to decide with confidence. So Table 2 is undifferentiated counts only, and they did the careful split just for LCIE.

sections.heading: Zipf's law: a few words do most of the work

blocks.body: In any large corpus, a word's frequency is roughly **inversely proportional to its rank**: the 2nd most common word appears about half as often as the 1st, the 3rd about a third as often, and so on. frequency × rank ≈ constant.

blocks.title: What it looks like
blocks.body:
rank 1  'the'  ~ 60,000 per million
rank 2  'of'   ~ 30,000
rank 3  'and'  ~ 20,000
rank 10         ~  6,000
rank 100        ~    600

A handful of function words cover a huge share of all tokens;
a very long tail of words appears once or twice (the hapaxes from Week 3).

blocks.md: **Why it matters for you** It means most words are rare. A 15,000-word corpus will have most content words at 0 or 1 hits, which is why the tiny-corpus trap above bites so hard, and why comparing two corpora needs a statistic, not eyeballing.

blocks.prompt: If the most frequent word in a corpus has 50,000 hits, roughly how many would Zipf's law predict for the 5th most frequent?

sections.heading: Keyness: what makes this corpus different

blocks.body: How much **more frequent** (or less) a word is in a **target** corpus than in a larger **reference** corpus, measured with a statistic (usually **log-likelihood**). Dr. Kraus's definition: 'words that are statistically more prominent, frequent, or significant in a target text or corpus compared to a larger reference corpus'. It is a measure of **statistical salience**.

blocks.md: Frequency lists tell you what is common. **Keyword** lists tell you what is *characteristic*. *the* is the most frequent word everywhere, so it is never key. Farr & Murphy ran a keyword list on their female talk corpus against a reference corpus, and six religious words came out in the top 20 (*God* was number 1). That was their first signal that something was going on.

blocks.title: Log-likelihood, step by step
blocks.body:
a = hits in target      = 90   (target size c = 45,000)
b = hits in reference   = 600  (reference size d = 1,000,000)

Expected, if the word were equally common everywhere:
  E1 = c × (a + b) / (c + d) = 45,000 × 690 / 1,045,000 = 29.7
  E2 = d × (a + b) / (c + d) = 1,000,000 × 690 / 1,045,000 = 660.3

LL = 2 × ( a·ln(a/E1) + b·ln(b/E2) )
   = 2 × ( 90·ln(90/29.7) + 600·ln(600/660.3) )
   = 84.6

LL above 3.84 → significant at p < 0.05; above 6.63 → p < 0.01.
84.6 is far above: this word is KEY in the target.

blocks.md: Read it in plain words: we **expected** about 30 hits in the target if it talked like the reference; we **saw** 90. Log-likelihood measures how surprising that gap is, taking both corpus sizes into account. The bigger the number, the more surprising.

blocks.body: Key does not mean frequent. A word can be key with only a few dozen hits if the reference almost never uses it, and a very frequent word is often not key at all. And 'statistically significant' does not tell you *why*; you still go back to the concordance.

blocks.prompt: True or false: keyness is a measure of statistical salience.
blocks.answer: True (that was the Week 5 Thursday quiz question). It measures how unexpectedly frequent a word is in the target compared with the reference.

blocks.md: Once you can normalize and test, you can compare **groups of speakers**. Farr & Murphy compared age groups and men vs women, all per million.

rows: Religious references are mostly an informal-speech thing
LCIE 1528, teen London talk 1322, vs academic 204–397 and US political 85 (Table 2)
Oldest speakers use them most, and more often in the religious sense
Men use them more, and the 'stronger' ones
total MAC 12,992 vs FAC 9,793; Christ 3199 vs 666 (Table 9)
Oh my God is a young-female cluster

blocks.title: Farr & Murphy's main results

blocks.md: **The other reading (Benor & Levy 2006)** does the same kind of work for word order: in binomials like *salt and pepper* or *ladies and gentlemen*, which word comes first? They count real binomials in corpora and model the ordering as **probabilistic** preferences (meaning, sound/rhythm, frequency) rather than strict rules. Same toolkit, different question.

blocks.prompt: A table says women in their 40s use 'Almighty' at 266 per million, in a 15,000-word sub-corpus. How many times did anyone actually say it?
blocks.answer: 266 × 15,000 ÷ 1,000,000 ≈ 4 times. Worth remembering before drawing big conclusions.

exercises.title: Normalize and compare
exercises.prompt: 'Jesus' occurs 462 times in the 1-million-word LCIE, and 22 times in a 500,000-word corpus of London teen talk. Which group uses it more, per million?
hints: LCIE is already 1 million words, so its count is its per-million rate.
solution: The Irish speakers use it about ten times as often.
exercises.why: Normalizing is the one step that makes every other comparison honest; forgetting it is the most common error in student corpus projects, including final papers.

exercises.title: Is it key?
exercises.prompt: A word appears 20 times in your 45,000-word target corpus and 400 times in a 1,000,000-word reference. Expected counts come out to E1 = 18.1 and E2 = 401.9. The log-likelihood is 0.20. Is the word key?
hints: Compare what you saw with what you expected in the target: 20 vs 18.1.
solution: Observed 20 vs expected 18.1: almost the same.
The word is not key; the target uses it at about the same rate as the reference (444 vs 400 per million).
exercises.why: Keyword lists are how corpus linguists find what to look at first. Knowing when a difference is just noise keeps you from building a paper on four lucky hits.

choices.feedback: Right: observed and expected are nearly equal.

choices.text: Yes, it appears more per million in the target
choices.feedback: 444 vs 400 per million is a small gap; the test says it could easily be chance.
